summary: The ipn URI scheme names endpoints in the interplanetary Bundle Protocol, used for delay-tolerant networking. This RFC updates its specification from RFC 6260 and the registries from RFC 7116. It also updates how the URIs are encoded and decoded when used as endpoint identifiers in Bundle Protocol version 7 (RFC 9171).

eli5.summary: Mail sent across space needs addresses. This updates the address format used to name places that data can be delivered in a network built for very long delays.

subtitle: Adds allocators, special node numbers and a compact three-element encoding to the ipn URI scheme used by Bundle Protocol nodes.

tldr.problem: The ipn URI scheme names nodes and services with plain integers for networks with limited power, bandwidth or compute, but growing Bundle Protocol deployments exposed gaps in how the scheme was structured, managed and encoded.
tldr.mechanism: Every ipn URI becomes a tuple of Allocator Identifier, Node Number and Service Number. IANA is the Default Allocator with identifier 0, special node numbers are defined, and BPv7 endpoint identifiers may use either a two-element or a new three-element CBOR encoding.
tldr.outcome: Older ipn URIs stay valid, but implementations that do not support non-default allocators or the three-element encoding are not forwards compatible and will reject such bundles as malformed.

today: RFC 9758 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2025 that updates RFC 6260, RFC 7116 and RFC 9171. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: What the ipn Scheme Is For
sections.content:
The ipn URI scheme was defined in RFC 6260 and RFC 7116 to identify network nodes and node services with concisely encoded integers that are cheaper to process than verbose identifiers. It was designed for the experimental Bundle Protocol version 6 (BPv6), and "IPN" originally stood for InterPlanetary Network. The RFC now treats it as a non-acronymous name, since integer identifiers suit any network with limited power, bandwidth or compute.

The standardized Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7) in RFC 9171 supports ipn URIs as Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs). Growth in BPv7 deployments highlighted areas to improve. This document introduces a hierarchical structure for assignment, clarifies behavior, defines efficient encodings and updates the registries, all in a backwards-compatible way.

An ipn URI is only an identifier. It carries no topological information about how to route messages to the resource.
sections.eli5: The ipn scheme gives places in a very slow, very far-flung network short number names, a bit like phone extensions.

sections.title: Allocators, Nodes and Services
sections.content:
Every ipn URI is a tuple of three parts: the Allocator Identifier, the Node Number and the Service Number. The allocator is the organization that assigns Node Numbers, so there is no need for one registry covering every node. The node number is shared by all resources on one node, and the service number tells resources on that node apart.

Allocator Identifiers are unique unsigned integers assigned by IANA. An allocator may hold several identifiers, but one identifier belongs to a single allocator. Organizations with internal hierarchies can receive a consecutive range, inspired by CIDR. A range must have a size that is a power of 2 and its first identifier must have the low bits all zero, so ranges can be compared with bitwise operations.

IANA is the Default Allocator, with Allocator Identifier 0, and an implementation MUST assume the default allocator when none is given. The pair of allocator and node number is the Fully Qualified Node Number (FQNN), written for example as (977000,100). The RFC says the term FQNN MUST be used for that combination.
sections.eli5: The allocator is the company that hands out house numbers, the node is the house, and the service is a room inside it. Together they pick out exactly one room.

sections.title: Special Numbers and Text Syntax
sections.content:
The Null ipn URI has allocator, node and service all set to 0 and means "nowhere". A URI with allocator 0 and node 0 but a non-zero service number is invalid and MUST be treated as the Null URI. The LocalNode URI uses allocator 0 and node number 4294967295 to refer to a service on the local node, and the text form SHOULD use ! instead of the digits. Default Allocator node numbers 1 to 0x3FFF are Private Use, which is not guaranteed unique beyond one administrative domain, similar to private IPv4 address space.

The text form is ipn:[allocator.]node.service. Leading zeros MUST be omitted, and a zero allocator MAY be left out. The text syntax is given in ABNF, for example ipn:977000.100.1.
sections.eli5: Some numbers are reserved: one means "nowhere", one means "this very computer", and a block is for private use, like a house number that only makes sense inside your own village.

sections.title: Using ipn URIs as BPv7 Endpoint IDs
sections.content:
An ipn EID MUST identify a singleton endpoint, and all EIDs sharing one FQNN MUST refer to the same bundle processing node. The URIs dtn:none, ipn:0.0 and ipn:0.0.0 all refer to the BPv7 Null endpoint. A Service Number of 0 identifies the node's Administrative Endpoint, and non-zero numbers MUST NOT be used for that.

LocalNode EIDs are non-routable. A bundle with one as source or destination MUST NOT leave the local node, and externally received bundles featuring one MUST be discarded as invalid. They MUST NOT be published in a node directory or used in dynamic peer discovery. Private Use EIDs likewise MUST NOT cross administrative domains, so gateways must be configurable to enforce that.

A new IANA registry of well-known service numbers lets public services have pre-agreed default numbers, with ranges reserved for experimentation and Private Use.
sections.eli5: An address that means "this computer" must never be sent out to others, because for them it would mean a different computer.

sections.title: CBOR Encodings
sections.content:
In BPv7 the scheme-specific part is a CBOR array of two or three unsigned integers. In the two-element form the first element is the FQNN packed into a 64-bit integer, with the Allocator Identifier in the most significant 32 bits and the Node Number in the least significant 32 bits, followed by the Service Number. For ipn:977000.100.1 the FQNN is 0xEE868_00000064 and the encoding is 11 octets. This matches the encoding in RFC 9171 for the default allocator.

In the three-element form the elements are Allocator Identifier, Node Number and Service Number, giving 9 octets for the same example. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to use it, except that for the Default Allocator the two-element form is more concise and is RECOMMENDED instead.

Decoders tell the forms apart by array length. EID matching MUST use the decoded information, so different encodings of the same EID MUST be treated as equivalent. The formal syntax is given in CDDL.
sections.eli5: The same address can be written in a longer or shorter way. Computers must still understand that both ways point to the same place.

sections.title: Compatibility Pitfalls
sections.content:
Any ipn URI valid before this update remains valid, and the two-element encoding is compatible with RFC 9171. The new features are not forwards compatible: non-default allocators and three-element encodings must be supported by updated software. Existing implementations reject three-element bundles as malformed, so forwarding of valid bundles can fail.

Mitigations include a configuration option to use the two-element encoding for given destinations, and tunneling through gateway nodes. Heuristic guessing from incoming bundles and transcoding at intermediate nodes do not work, partly because the primary block is immutable and blocks may be covered by security blocks.

Non-default allocator identifiers MUST NOT be used with BPv6. Elements of an ipn URI MUST NOT be read as location or routing information, since EIDs are late-bound names.
sections.eli5: Old devices only know the short way to write addresses. If you send them the new long way, they think it is garbled and throw it away.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Endpoints are never guaranteed reachable, and BPv7 alone does not guarantee who runs them. Verifying the Block Integrity Block signature under BPSec (RFC 9172) is required for that. A maliciously built ipn EID could misdirect a bundle or fake a source, so receiving nodes should verify authenticity, for example with BPSec and TCPCLv4 with TLS (RFC 9174). LocalNode and Private Use EIDs that leak beyond their domain break uniqueness and could be abused. Examination of ipn URIs could support traffic analysis.

IANA created the "'ipn' Scheme URI Allocator Identifiers" and "Well-Known Service Numbers for BPv7" registries, and renamed "CBHE Node Numbers" to "'ipn' Scheme URI Default Allocator Node Numbers". The allocator identifier ranges 974848-978943 are an Example Range for documentation.
sections.eli5: Anybody can write any numbers on an envelope, so the receiver should check that the sender really is who the envelope says.
